reading.en: You could say modern society has developed with the aim of 'not having to wait'. Things we order arrive the next day, and we can watch films at home right away without going to the cinema. With an app, we instantly know the fastest train connection. We have seen waiting as wasted time and worked hard to reduce it. Not having to wait is certainly nice. But is waiting time really all wasted? When I was a child, my favourite manga magazine came out only once a month. During the month until the next issue, my friends and I talked again and again about what would happen next. I even imagined the next part and drew it. Looking back, that month was as much fun as the manga itself. Waiting leaves room for imagination. Because answers are not given right away, people think for themselves and build up their hopes. And what we get after waiting feels more precious than what we get at once. Of course, some waiting, like long waits at hospitals or for paperwork at city offices, should be reduced. I don't mean we should enjoy all waiting. What I want to say is: in our pursuit of convenience, are we giving up even the things we gain from waiting? Sometimes, instead of searching for the answer right away, we could try enjoying the time spent waiting.

grammar.en:
These days, far fewer people write letters. Email and messages are enough, and above all they are fast. Even so, I still send handwritten letters a few times a year.
It started with a letter from my grandmother when I was a student. The writing was a little shaky, but each character was written carefully. As I read it, I could almost see her sitting at her desk.
Something I could write in a few minutes by email can take over an hour as a letter. But precisely because of that time, I can think slowly about the other person.

The writer is describing how it felt while reading: it was as if she could see her grandmother.

The next sentence starts with ただ and suggests letters only for special times, so the writer does not intend to use letters for everything.

Several years have passed since working from home spread. Many people are happy that commuting time has gone and they have more time with their families. I felt that way at first too.
But after about six months, my work somehow stopped moving forward. When I thought about why, I realised that the small talk with colleagues had disappeared. At the office, new ideas often came from casual chats while making coffee. In online meetings, we close the screen as soon as the business is done. It is efficient, but there is no room for extra talk.
So our team created a 15-minute 'chat time' once a week where we don't talk about work at all. At first it was a bit embarrassing, but now everyone looks forward to it. Perhaps it is exactly the time that looks wasted that a team needs.

reading.en:
When you travel, something troublesome almost always happens. You miss a train, or your name isn't at a hotel you thought you had booked. When I was young, I made detailed plans before leaving so that such trouble wouldn't happen.
But one summer, I missed a bus in a village deep in the mountains and had to wait three hours for the next one. With nothing else to do, I went into a nearby diner, and the owner told me about the village's history and a waterfall that tourists hardly know about. In the end, going to see that waterfall became the best memory of the trip.
Since then, I try not to pack my plans too full. A trip that goes as planned is reassuring, but I think it is the unplanned events that make a trip special.

reading.en:
The other day, the vacuum cleaner I have used for ten years stopped working. When I took it to an electronics shop, the clerk said, 'It's cheaper to buy a new one than to repair it.' Indeed, the repair would cost more than half the price of a new one.
Even so, I asked for it to be repaired. Partly I was attached to it, but I just couldn't accept throwing it away when so many parts could still be used.
I hear that some European countries are moving to require makers to keep parts for their products available for a long time. I hope a society will come where repairing things and using them for a long time is normal, not special.

I think elementary school children need homework. What you learn at school doesn't stick unless you practise it again and again at home. Also, the habit of sitting at a desk at a set time every day helps with study from junior high school on. However, too much homework makes children dislike studying, so an amount that takes about 30 minutes a day is best.
B
Recently, some elementary schools have stopped giving homework. They say it is so children can use their after-school time for things they are interested in. I agree. Even if everyone gets the same homework, it is too easy for some children and too hard for others. Children themselves should choose what to learn at home. Still, it goes without saying that reviewing at home what you learned at school is important.

reading.en:
When we talk with people, we tend to think only about what to say. Before speaking in a meeting we sort out our words in our heads, and even when chatting with friends we prepare our next line while the other person is talking. But perhaps whether a conversation goes well depends more on listening than on speaking.
I used to work in sales. When I had just joined the company, I believed products would sell if I explained their good points hard. But my results didn't improve. One day I went with a senior colleague to a sales meeting and was surprised. He hardly explained the product at all; for more than 40 minutes of the hour he listened to the customer: the company's situation, its problems, its future plans. He just nodded and sometimes asked short questions. At the end he said only, 'In that case, this product may be of help.' The customer signed the contract on the spot.
On the way back, he said, 'People trust someone who really listened to them.' If you don't know what the other person truly wants, no explanation, however skilled, will reach their heart. I was made to realise that I had been talking not for the customer but for what I wanted to sell.
Still, listening is not easy. When someone talks for a long time, you want to cut in. When you hear a different opinion, you want to argue back. To listen, you need the patience to put aside what you want to say for a while.
Nowadays anyone can freely share opinions on social media. Chances to speak have increased, but chances to listen seem to have decreased. That is exactly why I think what we need now is not skill in speaking well but an attitude of listening to the other person's words until the end.
